title: VLOOKUP with Multiple Criteria
description: VLOOKUP only matches one column, but real lookups often need two or more. Learn four reliable ways to do a VLOOKUP with multiple criteria in Excel and Google Sheets.
intro: A classic complaint about VLOOKUP is that it can only search one column. In practice you often need to match on two keys at once — for example, find the price for Product A in Region North. This guide walks through four techniques, from a quick helper column to the modern XLOOKUP approach, so you can pick the one that fits your Excel version.
prerequisites: Understanding of absolute vs relative references
Microsoft 365 (only needed for the XLOOKUP method)

sections.title: Why VLOOKUP Alone Falls Short
sections.content: VLOOKUP takes a single lookup_value and searches the first column of your table. If your match depends on two columns — say Product and Region — there is no second lookup_value to pass. The fix is to combine the keys into one value VLOOKUP can match.
tips: Keep the combined key in the FIRST column of the lookup table.
Both the search value and the table key must use the same join order.

sections.title: Method 1: Helper Column (Most Compatible)
sections.content: Add a column that concatenates the two keys, then VLOOKUP that combined value. This works in every version of Excel and Google Sheets.

steps.name: Build the key
steps.text: In a new first column of your table, join the two criteria.

steps.name: Lookup the joined key
steps.text: Concatenate your two search cells the same way in the VLOOKUP.

example.result: Returns the row where column A = G2 AND column B = H2
example.explanation: Because the first column is A&B, only rows matching BOTH criteria produce a hit.

tips: Use a delimiter like A2&"|"&B2 if keys could run together (e.g. 'AB'+'C' vs 'A'+'BC').

sections.title: Method 2: CHOOSE + VLOOKUP (No Helper Column)
sections.content: CHOOSE({1,2}, range1&range2, returnRange) builds a virtual two-column table on the fly, letting VLOOKUP match the concatenated key without editing your sheet.

example.result: Returns column D for the matching combined key
example.explanation: In legacy Excel this is an array formula — confirm with Ctrl+Shift+Enter. In Microsoft 365 it spills automatically.

tips: Whole-column references (A:A) in array formulas can be slow; restrict to your data range.

sections.title: Method 3: INDEX + MATCH (Recommended Classic)
sections.content: INDEX returns a value from a range; MATCH finds the row. Multiplying two TRUE/FALSE conditions inside MATCH gives an exact two-criteria match without any helper column.

example.result: Returns the column D value where A = G2 and B = H2
example.explanation: MATCH(1, ...) finds the first row where both conditions are TRUE (1). Array-enter in legacy Excel.

tips: INDEX + MATCH also looks LEFT, something VLOOKUP can never do.

sections.title: Method 4: XLOOKUP (Microsoft 365 / Google Sheets)
sections.content: XLOOKUP accepts array conditions directly, so multiple criteria are just AND-ed inside the lookup_value. This is the cleanest solution if your version supports it.

example.result: Returns the column D value matching both criteria
example.explanation: No array-entry, no helper column, and you can return multiple columns by widening the return array.

tips: Add a 4th argument, like "Not found", to handle missing combinations gracefully.

summary: VLOOKUP can't natively match two columns, but you have options: a helper column for maximum compatibility, CHOOSE for a no-edit workaround, INDEX + MATCH for a robust classic formula, and XLOOKUP when your version allows. Pick the helper column or XLOOKUP for day-to-day work, and keep INDEX + MATCH in your back pocket for leftward lookups.
